source.title_on_document: NexusAI: Enabling Design Space Exploration of Ideas through Cognitive Abstraction and Functional Decomposition

supplement.where: Appendices A-G, pp. 13-19 of this PDF; interaction-event Figure 14 on p. 21.
supplement.holds: Formative-study participant tables and workshop details; system prompts, implementation details and interaction illustrations; user-study participant demographics, questionnaires and interview guide. Appendix G, Table 4 (p. 19) reports structural-network means, p-values and r effect sizes, including the maximum-width result. Table 4 supplies no standard errors or confidence intervals.

paper_design_summary: A system paper on NexusAI, an LLM diagramming tool developed through formative interviews (conflicting participant counts) and a qualitative FigJam workshop with six creative practitioners (pp. 3-4, 13). In the main within-subject comparison, 14 practitioners completed two 20-minute future-design tasks, one using NexusAI and one using a baseline with the same LLM; tasks and conditions were counterbalanced, without stated randomization (pp. 6-8). The evaluations examine qualitative accounts, self-reported support and logged exploration-graph structure, with no reported creativity scores on designs or diversity scores across different people's outputs (pp. 3-4, 8-10, 19).

assignment.what_was_assigned: Which task (A: personal focus assistant, B: community memory archive) each participant did with NexusAI and which with the baseline; two counterbalanced groups of seven. The paper does not say how people were placed in the groups or which condition came first.
assignment.quote: Task order and condition assignments were balanced within two groups: seven participants completed Task A with NexusAI and Task B with the baseline; the remaining seven completed Task A with the baseline and Task B with NexusAI.
assignment.locator: p. 8, Section 5.2.3 (also p. 6, Section 5: "we conducted a within-subject study comparing two systems")

arms.name: NexusAI
arms.description: Graph-based diagramming system with the Cognitive Abstraction pipeline: decomposes LLM output into What-How-Value fragments, shifts abstraction levels, and recombines fragments across nodes.

arms.name: Baseline
arms.description: Node-based diagramming canvas with basic AI node generation, same LLM, same prompt templates, and same turn-based generation (pp. 7-8, Section 5.2.2; Figure 12). Section 5 (p. 6) instead calls it a conventional dialogue-based LLM interface.

participants.who: Practitioners recruited by purposeful sampling through practitioner communities (10 female, 4 male, aged 24-33); at least one year of LLM use; backgrounds in design, research, art, and engineering. Table 3 (p. 18) lists 13 rows (no ID 9).
participants.quote: Fourteen participants (Appendix E.1, Table 3; 10 female, 4 male; aged 24-33, M=27.1, SD=2.66) were recruited via purposeful sampling through practitioner communities.

ai_tool.name_model: Qwen-Plus via Alibaba DashScope API, text-embedding-v4 for retrieval and clustering (p. 6, Section 4.3); Appendix F (p. 19) instead says GPT-5.2 and text-embedding-ada-002 via Azure were used in the system implementation
ai_tool.how_used: Participants generated AI idea nodes and, in NexusAI, analyzed, transformed, and merged them into fragments on a diagram canvas; the baseline offered basic AI node generation on a canvas.

task.description: Open-ended future-design exploration: Task A, a future personal focus assistant; Task B, a future community memory archive.
task.duration: 20 minutes per task; session about 90 minutes

assignment.what_was_assigned: No experimental condition assignment is described. Participants were purposefully recruited for interviews about prior LLM-assisted design practices and desired interactions (p. 3, Section 3.1).
assignment.quote: we conducted semi-structured interviews with eight participants
assignment.locator: p. 3, Section 3.1, Participants and Procedure and Analysis

participants.exclusions: Not stated; the conflicting participant counts are not explained as exclusions.
participants.who: Creators recruited through professional design networks and university departments, with design-project experience and at least one year of weekly LLM use. Section 3.1 reports eight interview participants, but Section 3.1.1 describes seven designers and Table 1 lists seven participant rows. The analyzed count is left null because the paper does not resolve this discrepancy.
participants.quote: Our formative study with seven designers revealed three interconnected challenges in LLM-assisted creative exploration.
participants.locator: p. 3, Sections 3.1 and 3.1.1; p. 13, Appendix A.1, Table 1

ai_tool.name_model: Specific models used in prior LLM interactions are not stated.
ai_tool.how_used: Participants supplied full records of prior LLM interactions and discussed their LLM-assisted design experience; no assigned AI intervention is described (p. 3, Section 3.1).

task.description: Semi-structured interviews about existing LLM-assisted creativity tools, prior AI-assisted design, expected interactions and future tools. Transcripts were analyzed through qualitative open coding; no creativity or diversity score on produced outputs is reported (p. 3, Sections 3.1 and 3.1.1).

assignment.what_was_assigned: Participants followed a FigJam workshop protocol comprising browsing, design exploration and an interview. No comparison conditions or randomized allocation are described (pp. 3-4, Section 3.2).
assignment.quote: After informed consent, participants accessed a FigJam board containing 20 domain-agnostic information snippets.

participants.who: Six creative practitioners recruited by purposeful sampling from diverse design domains, with regular LLM use; Table 2 lists six participants.
participants.quote: we conducted design workshops with six creative practitioners (4 female, 2 male; aged 25–30) recruited via purposeful sampling.
participants.locator: p. 3, Section 3.2, Workshop Protocol & Participants; p. 13, Appendix A.1, Table 2

ai_tool.name_model: No workshop LLM model is stated.
ai_tool.how_used: The workshop used supplied information snippets and What-How-Value fragments on a FigJam board. Participants had prior LLM experience, but live LLM use during the workshop and the snippets' model provenance are not specified (p. 3, Section 3.2).

task.description: Browse supplied information snippets, manipulate decomposed What-How-Value fragments using sticky notes, develop new ideas and discuss the process. Annotations and transcribed sessions were qualitatively coded for functional roles, abstraction levels and interaction sequences; no creativity or diversity scores on outputs are reported (pp. 3-4, Section 3.2; p. 13, Figure 7).
task.duration: Browsing: 10 minutes; design exploration: 30 minutes; interview: 20 minutes (p. 3, Section 3.2).

eligibility.reason: No study meets the core criteria. The main within-subject comparison analyzes 14 people (p. 7, Section 5.1; p. 19, Table 4); the formative interview sample is inconsistently reported as eight versus seven, and the workshop includes six people (p. 3, Sections 3.1-3.2; p. 13, Tables 1-2). These study samples are not combined, and each reported sample is below 50. Both main-study arms use generative AI, but counterbalancing does not establish randomized condition order or group placement (p. 8, Section 5.2.3). The formative studies report qualitative findings, while the main user study evaluates perceived support and interaction-graph structure; no study reports creativity scored on designs or diversity across different people's outputs (pp. 3-4, 8-10, 19). Core remains no and context_class remains none.

one_line_finding: With 14 practitioners in a counterbalanced within-subject study, NexusAI produced wider, more branched exploration graphs than an LLM baseline (average out-degree 0.98 vs. 0.30, p = 0.004; max width 66.93 vs. 4.21, p = 0.001; Table 4, p. 19) and higher self-reported CSI (96.50 vs. 66.10, p = 0.020; p. 9), with no rated creativity of outputs.
